articles.title: A former Starbucks franchise boss built a tennis court on agricultural land in Hampshire; after years of objections, an inspector upheld enforcement action and gave him six months to remove the unauthorised works
articles.summary: A countryside property can be a private retreat, but transforming agricultural land into an elaborate leisure complex can bring planning rules into sharp
articles.body: A countryside property can be a private retreat, but transforming agricultural land into an elaborate leisure complex can bring planning rules into sharp focus. In Durley, near Southampton, a former Starbucks franchise executive’s ambitious garden makeover has ended in a planning setback after a three-year dispute. A planning inspector has backed Winchester City Council’s enforcement action, requiring the removal of the unauthorised tennis court and associated structures, alongside an end to the land’s unauthorised residential use, within six months.From countryside plot To leisure complexMark Hepburn, 53, purchased the property known as Cupressus for £740,000 in December 2017, according to The Sun. The six-bedroom home’s surrounding land was subsequently transformed with a range of recreational and residential features, including a bright blue tennis court, children’s playground, gym, bar and television room.The changes also included artificial grass, timber buildings and a gravel car park. The grounds reportedly housed a pen for the family’s pet micro-pigs and space for a flock of alpacas.However, the development attracted scrutiny from Winchester City Council, which maintained that the land was agricultural and could not lawfully be used as an extension of the residential garden. Hepburn argued that previous owners had used the land as a garden for years, but retrospective planning permission was refused twice before the council issued an enforcement notice, states another report by The Independent.Neighbours raise concernsThe development became a source of tension among neighbouring residents, who raised concerns about noise, lighting, changes to the landscape and the impact on local wildlife.According to The Sun, residents complained about late-night parties, outdoor discos and lights that remained on overnight, illuminating the tennis court, swimming pool and other parts of the property. Some also alleged that mature trees had been removed and that fencing had affected the movement of wildlife, including badgers, deer and foxes.Other neighbours expressed concern about the effect of the development on the area's rural appearance, pointing to the brightly coloured court, playground and additional buildings as a departure from the previously open countryside, states another report by Daily Mail.These objections formed part of a wider planning dispute over whether the land’s transformation was compatible with its agricultural status and surrounding landscape.Planning inspector upholds enforcementIn its official statement, Winchester City Council confirmed that a planning inspector had dismissed two linked appeals relating to the land at Cupressus, on Durley Brook Road.The inspector concluded that the unauthorised residential use of agricultural land and the associated development would harm the character of the countryside and conflict with relevant planning policies. The decision upheld the council’s enforcement action and dismissed a related planning appeal.The ruling grants Hepburn six months to comply with the enforcement notice. The required measures include removing the unauthorised tennis court and associated development, as well as ending the land’s unauthorised residential use.The council said its enforcement service had worked over several years to address the planning breaches and secure compliance with local planning controls.Business success meets planning rulesHepburn is known for co-founding 23.5 Degrees, described as the UK's first independent Starbucks franchise. According to The Sun, the business operated 115 outlets before it was sold in October 2014 in a deal reportedly valued at around £140 million.The outcome at Cupressus underlines the distinction between owning private land and having permission to change how it is used.Winchester City Council said it would continue working with the landowner to ensure the necessary action is completed within the inspector’s six-month deadline. The decision also reinforces the council’s stated commitment to taking proportionate enforcement action against unauthorised development.For Hepburn, the ruling marks a significant setback in a prolonged planning dispute. For the council, it confirms that agricultural land and the character of the surrounding countryside remain subject to planning controls, even when extensive changes have already been made.Image Courtesy: istockYou use AI every day. articles.title: US accuses government contractor of leaking classified info to girlfriend's Substack
articles.summary: Oct 23 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department accused a government contractor on Friday of leaking national defense information to his girlfriend, the publish...
articles.body:
Oct 23 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department accused a government contractor on Friday of leaking national defense information to his girlfriend, the publisher of a Substack newsletter.

The FBI arrested Ian Brinksman, ‌42, on Friday following a search of his Washington home, a Justice Department statement said. Prosecutors charged ‌him with unlawfully transmitting national defense information.

A federal public defender representing Brinksman declined to comment.

"As alleged, Brinksman reached far outside his own duties ​to obtain some of our Nation's most closely held secrets and handed them to a romantic partner he knew intended to publish them," John Eisenberg, assistant attorney general for national security, said in the statement.

"That is not carelessness. It is a betrayal of his oath and the American people who entrusted him to fulfill his duties honorably," Eisenberg ‌said.

Brinksman held a top secret security clearance ⁠while working as an employee of a US government agency and later as a developer for systems integration for a private contractor working for the same agency, prosecutors said.

According ⁠to the sworn affidavit of an FBI agent investigating the case, Brinksman repeatedly accessed classified intelligence reports and then communicated with the journalist. The affidavit also cites phone records, database access logs, badge-swipe records, emails and other evidence.

The affidavit only ​identifies ​the journalist as "Individual 1," but it cites excerpts from articles ​she published.

"A fundraising article reportedly published by ‌Individual 1 in September 2026 stated 'over the past year (Individual 1 has) published reporting based on classified (relevant U.S. government agency) assessments that I believe the public deserves to know about,'" the affidavit reads.

That quote appears in a September 28 piece published on the Capital & Empire online newsletter authored by Aída Chávez.

"Over the past year, I've published reporting based on classified CIA assessments that I believe the public deserves to know about," wrote Chávez, whose profile on the site ‌notes that she worked for the Nation and other outlets ​before she launched the newsletter.

Chávez did not respond to an email ​message seeking comment.

Investigators allege that on at least ​five occasions in 2026, Individual 1 published Substack articles containing information that mirrored the classified reports, ‌some at the top secret level. On some ​of those dates, Chávez published ​articles that cite classified reports, some of them attributed to the CIA.

According to a LinkedIn profile bearing Brinksman's name, he worked for Deloitte as a manager and as a senior strategy security consultant after having ​worked as a US State Department ‌foreign service officer on dates corresponding to those outlined in the Justice Department statement.

The State Department ​declined to comment. Deloitte did not respond to requests for comment.

(Reporting by Daniel Trotta in Carlsbad, ​California; Editing by Tom Hogue, Sergio Non, Rod Nickel)

articles.summary: A knife-wielding woman was shot by police after multiple people were stabbed during a violent incident inside a home in Queens, New York, on Friday night,
articles.body: A knife-wielding woman was shot by police after multiple people were stabbed during a violent incident inside a home in Queens, New York, on Friday night, according to police. Four people, including the woman and three men, suffered stab wounds in the incident.The incident took place at a residence on 149th Street in the Jamaica neighbourhood, with emergency services arriving at around 9:38 pm following reports of a stabbing, the New York Post reported. The woman was taken to Jamaica Hospital in stable condition, while the injured men were taken to two different hospitals, police said.According to NYPD Chief of Patrol Philip Rivera, a wounded man inside the house told officers through a second-floor window that his uncle had stabbed him and warned them against entering the residence. The circumstances surrounding the injuries to the other victims remain unclear.Police said the woman threw keys out of a third-floor window, allowing officers to enter the house. Once inside, they heard screams coming from the third floor and rushed to a small bedroom, where they found two men and the woman involved in a struggle.Rivera said one man was sitting on the floor, another was on top of him, and the woman was on top of both men. Officers ordered all three to raise their hands, following which the individuals separated.While the two men complied, the woman refused to raise her right hand and pointed towards one of the men across the room with her left hand, Rivera said. She then moved towards the officers while holding a knife.The woman was within a few feet of the officers when one of them opened fire, hitting her. Another officer deployed a Taser after she fell to the ground, Rivera said.Officers then took the woman downstairs and performed lifesaving measures before rushing her to Jamaica Hospital. One of the injured men was also taken to the same hospital, while the other two men were transported to North Shore University Hospital.Police recovered two serrated kitchen knives at the scene. The investigation remains ongoing, and officers have cordoned off the street.A nearby resident told the New York Post that a family with teenage children lives at the house where the incident took place.Another neighbour, identified as 60-year-old Rosie, said she had never witnessed anything like the incident in her three decades living in the area.Rosie told the newspaper that she had returned from visiting her husband at a hospital in Long Island and was unable to reach her home because police had blocked the street. articles.title: Plymouth murder charge after body found in wheelie bin
articles.summary: Police say Mohamed Abotaka, 36, is charged with the murder of 52-year-old Ali Barzai.
articles.body:
A man has been charged with murder after a body was found partially within a wheelie bin, police have said.

Devon and Cornwall Police said Mohamed Abotaka, 36, of Grand Parade, Plymouth, was charged with the murder of 52-year-old Ali Barzai. The force said Abotaka was due to appear in court on Monday.

Police said Barzai's body was found in a service lane off Grand Parade at about 06:40 BST on Wednesday.

Det Insp Chris Lithgow urged people not to speculate and said a heightened police presence would remain in the area in the coming days.

The force said Abotaka remained in police custody, and urged anyone with information to get in touch.

It added inquiries were ongoing to locate Barzai's next-of-kin.

articles.title: Canada won’t see Alberta seceding anytime soon. But what to do with the people who wanted to leave?
articles.summary: In the end, it wasn’t even close. Alberta’s preliminary referendum results were a definitive rejection of the idea that the province would be better off as an independent country.
articles.body: In the end, it wasn’t even close. Alberta’s preliminary referendum results were a definitive rejection of the idea that the province would be better off as an independent country. By a 3-to-1 margin, the province chose to remain in Canada and said “no” to a second, binding vote on secession. Nonetheless, separatist activist Jeffrey Rath was rather cheerful when he spoke to CNN the morning after the loss. “We don’t see this as a setback,” Rath said Tuesday. “For a fledgling political movement, it was a major accomplishment and a hell of a victory.” About a fourth of voters – over 500,000 Albertans – wanted another vote, the first step on a pathway towards secession from Canada. What now for them? Despite their loss, the over half a million people that voted for a binding plebiscite on independence are here to stay, said Dr. Jared Wesley, a political scientist at the University of Alberta. And it will be worth watching what they turn their efforts to next. “Separatism may have been rejected in Alberta, but they’ll move onto something else,” said Wesley, who spoke throughout the campaign in favor of staying in Canada. “Alberta separatism is only one element of a much broader, far-right populist movement in Canada.” Wesley pointed out that the independence referendum wasn’t the only question on the ballot earlier this week. There were also five separate non-binding referenda about immigration, including whether the provincial government ought to take “increased control” and whether Alberta should require proof of citizenship to vote. With the unofficial results out, all appear to have passed. “Alberta separatists have far more in common with the MAGA movement than they do with secessionist movements across the globe,” Wesley said. “They may lose on one issue, but they don’t go away. They adapt. They find another issue, and they seem to have found one on immigration.” The movement has been complicated by its ties to right-wing politics in the United States, with high profile voices like US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and SpaceX founder Elon Musk egging them on. Cory Morgan, who founded the Alberta Independence Party in 2000, told CNN that he has learned from the referendum that most people in Alberta simply did not want to separate. “The movement just isn’t ready, to be blunt,” Morgan said. But he also argues that calls for separatism were overshadowed by the trade war with the United States and US President Donald Trump’s threats to annex Canada. Numerous separatists – including Rath himself – made trips to Washington to meet with members of the Trump administration looking for support — a tactic that may have backfired back home. “It led to mistrust,” Morgan said. “I think that factor really did hinder the movement’s growth this year.” Rath dismissed this analysis, saying that his meetings with the Trump administration were “very useful” for shoring up US support in case independence was achieved, and that people who were nervous about his movement’s high-level interactions with the US were being needlessly sensitive. “Do people have a lot of ‘Trump derangement syndrome’ in Canada? Yeah,” Rath said. “What can I say? It doesn’t take a lot to trigger them, and I’ll be frank – I’ve almost gone out of my way to trigger a lot of them.” Yet other separatist movements in Canada appear to have taken the hint. Quebec’s Parti Quebecois, which took control of the provincial legislature with just under a third of the vote, has pledged not to hold an independence referendum while Trump is president. “Fear of United States annexation placed a huge cap on people’s willingness to take a chance at dividing Canada,” said Wesley, the political scientist. “The relationship with the United States was front and center in people’s minds as they were voting.” Though Morgan thinks the independence movement isn’t ready to take another big swing, he thinks that the 500,000 votes that it earned on Monday are a good start. “This was a solid base that said they’re ready to look at that option,” Morgan said. “And it’s not going away.”

articles.title: More than 1,000 arrested in France as protestors and police clash
articles.summary: While demonstrations throughout France were largely peaceful, police reported clashes with protesters Saturday evening.
articles.body:
Nearly 1,000 people were arrested in nationwide protests in France, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said Saturday, after demonstrations over the high cost of living and the country's education system earlier in the day remained largely peaceful.

Nuñez said the number of arrests is expected to rise significantly. He said marches "passed off well" in cities, but police officers found themselves confronted with "an extremely elevated level of violence" from "ultra-left" groups later in the day. Nuñez said some shops and businesses had been looted, but "the scale was far smaller" than a week earlier, when some 3,000 businesses were damaged or looted.

He said police acted more rapidly and conducted more pre-demonstration checks. Businesses and shopping centers had also been better protected. Earlier Saturday, the interior minister said police had confiscated weapons including metal balls, lead pellets, fireworks, slingshots, steel balls, improvised weapons, a katana and airsoft weapons, he said.

The French Interior Ministry said about 410,000 people participated in about 298 protests around the country . Union organizers from the General Confederation of Labor put the number at around 800,000. An explanation for the discrepancy was not immediately available.

Some confrontations were reported between authorities and demonstrators in several cities, but as of Saturday evening there had been no repeat of the major street violence and rioting that erupted amid similar protests last week.

Nuñez previously said that French authorities were preparing to maintain order this weekend by maintaining up to 70,000 officers nationwide along with assets including helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons.

Nuñez said authorities will remain "on high alert" overnight and into Saturday.

Clashes break out in Paris after largely peaceful march

Paris had prepared for unrest, with shops boarded up and events including those related to the NFL's first French football game canceled, but authorities described the atmosphere in the city as "calm."

Thousands gathered at the Porte d'Italie on the city's southeastern rim for an authorized demonstration. The march had originally been set for the Bastille, near the city's center, and was changed to the more remote Porte d'Italie at the last minute. Union representative Murielle Guilbert told reporters that it was "scandalous" that Macron had forbidden protesters from demonstrating "where we wish to demonstrate," but participants complied with the change.

The front of the march ended without incident. Some chanted "We are not happy" as they peeled away from the Porte de Vincennes. Police said 110,000 people participated in the event, while union members put the number at 250,000.

As the evening went on, clashes were reported between police and demonstrators, the Agence France-Presse reported. Nuñez said that "several thousand radical activists" had "gathered at the rear of the march, including around 500 individuals identified as rioters."

Clashes between protesters and police lasted about two hours, he said.

The Paris prosecutor's office said 64 people, including six minors, were arrested and 40 were placed in police custody. Most arrests concerned suspected weapons offenses or participation in a group preparing violence or property damage, the office said. More than 3,000 were stopped and checked by officers, police said.

Protesters march against far-right gathering

In Orleans, thousands of people marched against a congress held by Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally party. Le Pen is launching her campaign to succeed Emmanuel Macron as France's president. Elections will be held in six months, and surveys show Le Pen is best-placed to win. Demonstrators in Orleans protested both Macron and Le Pen.

"Macron resign. Le Pen in prison," the crowd yelled, according to the AFP. Police put their numbers at 11,000, while organizers said 26,000 took part. About 50 organizations, including labor unions, left-wing parties and student groups, had called for a protest against Le Pen's nationalist, anti-immigration party.

Some placards seen at the march referenced a shooting in Trappes , a Paris suburb, that left one person dead and several others injured across several locations. Macron called the rampage a "racist terror attack." Prosecutors are investigating the shooting as a terrorist incident.

French media reported that the protest against the congress ended peacefully early Saturday afternoon. The gathering is expected to continue through Sunday.

Protesters and police clash in smaller cities

Demonstrations had been banned in the southeast city of Lyon, but about 150 protesters near the city's center briefly tried to block a road. Police fired tear gas to disperse the group. Tear gas was also used to break up a group of around 1,000 people gathered in the south of the city. Street fires were also reported.

A police helicopter was seen flying over the city, and security forces, armored vehicles and riot police vans were patrolling. A 21-year-old student, who spoke to the Agence France-Presse on the condition of anonymity, described authorities as "really mobile."

In the western city of Nantes, thousands of protesters broke through police lines to enter the city center, the AFP reported. Officers used tear gas and a water cannon to try and disperse them. Some on the fringes of the demonstration threw projectiles and aimed fireworks at officers.

Police said about 17,000 attended an event in Marseille. Officers fired tear gas during clashes with several dozen people near the march's endpoint. Street fires were seen in the city.

Tear gas was also deployed in Clermont-Ferrand, Bordeaux and Strasbourg, police said. Nuñez said one person was seriously injured in Clermont-Ferrand, but did not provide any details.

In the city of Toulouse, a 20-year-old man reportedly had fingers blown off, Nuñez said. He did not provide more details about the person, their condition, or how they came to be injured.

Nuñez said that in the southern cities of Cannes and Montpellier, authorities saw far-right activists who claimed they were there to protect businesses or sought confrontations with "ultra-left militants." He said it was the first time authorities witnessed this phenomenon.

In Nice, where demonstrations had also been banned, 11 people were arrested after far-right extremists fought with demonstrators downtown, regional authorities said. Water cannons were also used in the city.

Organizers call for Halloween demonstrations

One group of protesters, the Yellow Vests, said they would hold another round of protests on Oct. 31. The Yellow Vests emerged about eight years ago as a loosely organized group that staged disruptive protests against Macron.

Organizers called for rallies and a sit-in outside parliament and city halls nationwide, condemning the "authoritarian drift" of Macron's government and urging citizens to stand up for "public freedoms."

The demonstrations have been ongoing since September, when high school students in the southeast of Paris protested for better conditions. The unrest quickly spread across the country as people took to the streets to demand relief from rising living costs.

Other protests are expected across Europe on Saturday, encompassing a broad range of issues including pensions, housing costs, anti-war movements, education and corruption.

Italy deployed soldiers to Milan, the nation's fashion and finance capital, as the city braced for fresh demonstrations one week after looting and police clashes. Many stores were boarded up with wooden planks on Saturday. Premier Giorgia Meloni announced a raft of measures, including sending an additional 500 soldiers to Milan and tougher penalties for minors, who police said made up a large part of the violent protesters.

In Rome, authorities locked down luxury shopping streets and stepped up patrols around key sites. Several hundred students demonstrated peacefully in the historic city. Organizers of peaceful events sought to distance themselves from potential unrest, urging participants to keep their faces uncovered and their hands visible.

In Albania's capital of Tirana, riot police used water cannons to subdue large groups of protesters. Some of the demonstrators threw projectiles at police, the AP reported. A separate protest organized by the opposition outside the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama turned violent earlier Saturday, with some activists lighting fires on the street. The demonstrators are mainly high school and university students, demanding lower tuition fees, greater state investment in education and protesting corruption in the education system. A broader anti-government movement is calling for Rama's resignation.

In Spain, thousands of retirees and others marched through central Madrid to demand that public pensions aren't meddled with.

Protesters in Lisbon, Portugal, are expected to march across the city Saturday to demand affordable housing.

articles.title: Thousands of Israelis rally against Netanyahu gov’t days before election
articles.summary: Opposition figures join Tel Aviv protesters demanding an independent October 7 inquiry.
articles.body:
Thousands of Israelis are protesting against the government and calling for an independent inquiry into the security failures that led to the October 7, 2023 attacks .

Demonstrators rallied in the public plaza known as Hostages Square in Tel Aviv on Saturday, three days before Israel’s first general election since the genocidal war on Gaza began.

The protest was organised by the October Council, a group founded by the families of captives taken to Gaza three years ago, to demand accountability for the government’s failure to prevent the Hamas attack that preceded the war.

“Three days before the election, we will hold the culminating event marking three years of struggle to uncover the truth, demand accountability and establish a state commission of inquiry,” the October Council wrote on X ahead of the rally.

Elsewhere in Israel, protesters were also gathering for antigovernment demonstrations, reported Haaretz newspaper.

Taking part were leading figures from opposition parties, including Gadi Eisenkot of the Yashar party, who is Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s main centre-right rival.

In Tel Aviv, Eisenkot was greeted by chants of “Who’s coming? The next prime minister”, according to The Times of Israel. The leader of the Democrats, Yair Golan, was also at the rally.

“Masses, masses of masses, flowing in the ‘Democrats’ march from Rabin Square to the Hostages Square – for change, for hope, for r-e-v-o-l-u-t-i-o-n. What energy. This time it’s ours completely!”, Israeli citizen and lawyer Dan Adin posted on X.

Polls ahead of Tuesday’s election suggest a tight race, with Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc, in power since late 2022, neck and neck with Eisenkot’s. Neither bloc is currently projected to obtain a majority of seats in Israel’s parliament.

The election could be pivotal in determining whether Israel launches another round of strikes on Iran. Eisenkot is believed to be less inclined to resume military action against Tehran if he becomes Israel’s next prime minister.

However, on most other foreign policy issues, leading Israeli parties and politicians remain united, including in their opposition to the creation of an independent Palestinian state.

Ahead of the protest, the October Council alerted law enforcement to possible “provocations” from pro-government agitators.

“We have sent an urgent letter to the Police Commissioner following alerts about attempts by entities linked to the coalition to disrupt tonight’s rally,” it wrote on X.

The October Council aims to hold Israeli officials deemed responsible for the October 7 attacks to account and deliver justice for affected families.

Netanyahu’s coalition government, however, has refused demands to establish an independent commission of inquiry. Instead, it has offered to set up a “political” commission. Half of the commission’s members would be appointed by the government, while the remainder would be appointed by opposition legislators.

Opposition leaders have said they would boycott a commission appointed by politicians.

articles.title: China urges US Treasury to stop proposed restrictions on tech investments
articles.summary: Chinese officials called on the U.S. Saturday to reconsider its proposed rule seeking to further restrict American investments into its tech industry, saying the move would disrupt trade relations between the two countries. On Thursday, the Treasury Department proposed a rule expanding existing restrictions in the Outbound Investment Security Program (OISP) on hypersonic systems, quantum…
articles.body:
Chinese officials called on the U.S. Saturday to reconsider its proposed rule seeking to further restrict American investments into its tech industry, saying the move would disrupt trade relations between the two countries.

On Thursday, the Treasury Department proposed a rule expanding existing restrictions in the Outbound Investment Security Program (OISP) on hypersonic systems, quantum information technologies, high-performance computing, supercomputing and AI. The proposed mandate seeks to prevent a handful of foreign adversaries — China, Russia and North Korea — from using money from the U.S. to bolster its own technological advancement.

Beijing’s commerce ministry firmly opposed the proposal in a statement published in the Chinese Global Times, a state run media outlet, in which a spokesperson said the rule “discriminatorily” widened China-related investment restrictions.

“This is a typical case of overstretching the concept of national security. China will closely monitor subsequent developments and reserves the right to take corresponding measures,” the spokesperson said.

The ministry also said the proposal would damage ⁠economic ties between the two countries, and it reserved the right to take unspecified ​countermeasures .

The new rule also adds the biotechnology industry to the list of sectors it plans to target under OISP, an addition Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for, according to a Thursday press release from the department .

“The proposed regulations would strengthen the existing Outbound Investment Security Program to prevent our adversaries from using U.S. investment to develop critical technologies that threaten U.S. national security,” Bessent said .

The proposal will go through a public comment period before the Treasury issues a final rule.

Earlier this week, the State Department announced sanctions against five Chinese companies connected to a former Google engineer , Linwei Ding, who was convicted earlier this year of stealing AI-related trade secrets. China opposed the sanctions , saying the punishment “severely harms the legitimate rights and interests” of Chinese businesses.

articles.title: Canadian University allows convicted murderer on day parole to attend law course, major outrage among students
articles.summary: McGill University in Montreal, Canada, is facing a growing controversy after a convicted murderer serving a life sentence began attending law classes
articles.body: McGill University in Montreal, Canada, is facing a growing controversy after a convicted murderer serving a life sentence began attending law classes while on day parole. The case has divided students over campus safety, the university's handling of the situation and whether a former prisoner should be allowed to continue his education as part of his rehabilitation.The dispute intensified after students raised concerns about the university's failure to inform them of the man's criminal history. An open letter called for restrictions on his campus access, while another group of students and alumni has urged the university to allow him to return to his studies.Who is the man at the centre of the controversy?The student is Jeffrey George Ewert, now in his 60s. He was convicted of second-degree murder and attempted murder following two violent attacks in British Columbia in 1984.According to a summary of his case in his parole board file, Ewert sexually assaulted and killed a woman and, less than six weeks later, beat and choked a 15-year-old girl, leaving her paralysed and permanently disabled.Ewert is serving a life sentence and was granted day parole in 2025 after spending about 40 years in prison. Day parole allows an eligible prisoner to live in the community under supervision and conditions while continuing to serve their sentence.He began attending classes at McGill's Faculty of Law in August 2026. He was also attending faculty events before the university controversy came to light.Parole documents cited in reporting say clinical assessments had placed his risk of reoffending in the moderate-to-high range. However, the documents indicated that close supervision in a halfway house and clinical follow-up could bring the assessed risk into the moderate category.Why are students demanding action?The controversy came into public view after students learned about Ewert's criminal history and questioned why the university had not informed them.Some students said they felt vulnerable because they had not known about his past. They argued that advance information about the situation and the safeguards in place would have helped them make informed decisions about interacting with him.An open letter from students called for the university to address concerns about campus safety, risk assessment and the absence of appropriate safeguards and consultation.The letter also made allegations about Ewert's behaviour on campus and online, including claims that he had been inappropriately physical with female students, some of whom were minors, and that his online activity reflected harmful attitudes towards women.Why are some students defending his right to study?Not everyone at McGill believes Ewert should be excluded from campus.A separate petition, drafted by three law students and signed by more than 100 students and alumni, argues that barring him from attending classes undermines his access to education and rehabilitation.The petition acknowledges concerns about student safety but argues that exclusion without a finding of misconduct or a conversation about the circumstances is unfair.“We are asking that Jeff be given the chance to do what the rest of us are doing, which is to attend class and learn,” the petition says.“A ban from the premises, with no conversation beforehand and no finding of misconduct, takes that chance away.”Annica Dickens, one of the petition's authors, said “public discomfort should not, on its own, be treated as proof that someone poses a threat.”She added: “His past is serious, and I don’t want to minimize the harm experienced by his victims or their families. But we also have to consider who he is today, his behaviour since then, and the safeguards that are in place.”What does his lawyer say?Ewert's lawyer, Nora Demnati, has said McGill knew about his criminal history and parole status when he applied to study law.She has described him as an example of rehabilitation and said his admission to the university followed years of legal advocacy while he was in prison.Demnati has also argued that information about his conduct should be considered in the context of his parole conditions and the supervision he receives.Following the publication of the students' allegations, she said Ewert shared the letter's contents with his parole supervisor and was working with his case management team.His parole conditions include restrictions on entering drinking establishments, requirements to report relationships with women and provisions allowing his case management team to access his telecommunications activity.Some of these conditions were introduced after concerns about his interactions with women online, including viewing social media profiles and using a dating site without informing his case management team.Demnati has argued that isolated information can lead to incomplete or prejudicial conclusions when considered without the full context.“Mr Ewert recognizes that his past has caused harm, and he understands that it can make people, particularly women, uncomfortable. That discomfort is legitimate and he does not minimize it. He also remains mindful of the harm caused to his victims,” his lawyer said.What has McGill University done?Ewert has not been on campus since October 6, 2026, and the university has been reviewing its response to the situation.McGill has declined to discuss the details of the individual case, citing privacy laws. It has said that criminal background checks are not typically part of Canadian universities' admissions processes.The university has also said it would act if concerning information about a student's background or behaviour were brought to its attention and would work with relevant government bodies where necessary.Provost Angela Campbell told the university community that a “fair process” was underway to balance the rights and interests of everyone involved.Law faculty dean Tina Piper also sought to reassure students, saying the university's priority was the safety and well-being of members of the faculty.You use AI every day. articles.title: ED moves Supreme Court against HC order to quash case against portal, founder
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Enforcement Directorate has moved Supreme Court against the Delhi high court’s order quashing the money-laundering case against digital news
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Enforcement Directorate has moved Supreme Court against the Delhi high court’s order quashing the money-laundering case against digital news platform NewsClick and its founder-editor Prabir Purkayastha, alleging that the HC committed a grave error by quashing the 2020 ECIR without examining the allegations against them.The directorate, which filed an appeal almost five months after the HC pronounced the order on May 29, also took the ground that the HC passed the order five months and 26 days after the judgement was reserved and it was in violation of SC’s guidelines that the verdict should be delivered within three months. “That, from a reading of the judgment it appears that due to the lapse of such period in pronouncing the judgment, several critical contentions raised by the prosecution were overlooked or left unaddressed by the high court,” the agency said.Giving details of the financial transaction of the news portal, it said the company was incorporated upon conversion from M/s PP Newsclick Studio LLP on Jan 11, 2018 and within three months, a loss-making company with hardly any assets received FDI worth Rs 9.6 crore by selling its shares for a premium at Rs 11,510/- per share.“PPK’s balance sheet for the FY 2018-19 reveals that it had assets worth only Rs 57 lakhs (approx.) and the company had suffered huge losses varying from Rs 37.8 lakh in FY 2017-18 to Rs.6.61 crore in FY 2018-19. No reason for any genuine investor to pay Rs. 11,510/- per share for a share whose face value was only Rs 10 at the time of allotment only 3 months back,” the appeal said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: A man was arrested Friday night near the Brooklyn set of “Miami Vice ‘85,” the film starring Michael B. Jordan and Austin Butler. Alex Perez, 23, of Brooklyn, was arrested just after 11 p.m. on accusations that he displayed a knife during a verbal dispute with another man in the area of Avenue N and McDonald Avenue, the New York City Police Department said. “The individual was then taken into custody without incident, and the knife was recovered,” the NYPD said. No one was injured. Perez was charged with menacing and criminal possession of a weapon. It was not immediately clear if he has retained an attorney. At the time, “Miami Vice ‘85,” a reboot of the beloved undercover detective drama, was filming along Bay Parkway and McDonald Avenue, near Washington Cemetery. Joseph Kosinski directs the film.

articles.title: Brazil’s Lula, Bolsonaro draw thousands to election-eve rallies
articles.summary: The pivotal run-off will determine whether Brazilians stick with their left-wing leader or shift towards the right.
articles.body:
Brazil’s presidential candidates Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro have rallied thousands of supporters in a final show of campaign strength in advance of the country’s closely contested run-off election.

Donning a red hat, Lula addressed hundreds of supporters at Rio de Janeiro’s Copacabana Beach on Saturday, waving a Brazilian flag from a campaign truck as crowds gathered on the final day of campaigning.

“The people must choose either someone who kisses the national flag or someone who kisses the American flag”, the 80-year-old told the crowd as he referenced his opponent’s ties to US President Donald Trump.

Lula is seeking a fourth, non-consecutive term in Sunday’s run-off, which will task Brazilians with determining whether to stick with their incumbent left-wing leader or join a broader regional shift towards the right.

Bolsonaro, a senator and son of former far-right President Jair Bolsonaro, secured 47 percent of the vote in the first round, narrowly ahead of Lula’s 45 percent.

Recent polling shows Lula and the younger Bolsonaro remain about even on the eve of the pivotal election.

A CNT/MDA survey released on Saturday revealed Bolsonaro would receive 46.3 percent of the vote compared ⁠with 45 percent for the left-wing ⁠Lula. Last week, ⁠the poll showed a slightly closer race with Bolsonaro leading ⁠Lula 46.8 percent to ⁠45.9 percent.

The poll’s margin of error was 2.2 ‌percentage ‌points.

On Saturday, Bolsonaro’s supporters, including hundreds of motorcyclists wearing Brazil’s yellow national football shirts, gathered in the southeastern state of Minas Gerais.

One of those supporters, Ebert Dorigo, accused Lula’s Workers’ Party (PT) of encouraging dependence on government welfare, arguing a change in direction was needed for the country.

“The values we uphold are nation and family. Our country is divided today because, due to welfare-based policies, some people … haven’t grasped that improvement and achievement come only through hard work,” he told the news agency AFP.

The bitter campaign has exposed deep divisions over economic policy, crime and Brazil’s political future, which Bolsonaro has pledged to tackle with hundreds of thousands of more spots in prison and cuts to government spending.

His father, who served as president from 2019 to 2022, is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup after losing that year’s election to Lula.

The two candidates struck a calmer tone during their final debate on Friday, although they traded accusations over the country’s economic difficulties and their respective records.

For some voters, however, the choice has been a difficult one.

“If there were any other candidate, that would be a better option,” Gabriela Ribeiro Viana, an event organiser, told AFP. “But we’re stuck choosing between the worst, the horrible, and the lesser evil”.

articles.title: Suspicious pigeon with coded ring, Pak currency causes a flutter in Jammu
articles.summary: JAMMU: A suspicious pigeon carrying a coded ring, a chit written in Urdu and Pakistani currency was caught by locals along the border in Jammu’s Samba
articles.body: JAMMU: A suspicious pigeon carrying a coded ring, a chit written in Urdu and Pakistani currency was caught by locals along the border in Jammu’s Samba district on Saturday, officials said.An official pointed out that such episodes are not uncommon in border areas of J&K and Punjab, where pigeons have been used for smuggling or for sending messages across the frontier.On Saturday, the pigeon was found near a temple in Samba’s border area of Mawa around 6.40am and was immediately captured by locals after they spotted a ring tied to its leg. “A ring bearing Code No 03341214150 was found attached to its leg, besides the note and currency,” the official said.A police team arrived soon and seized the pigeon with the items. “The pigeon has been taken for examination. Security agencies are verifying the contents of the note and the origin of the bird,” the official said.Suspicious creatures and items flying in are not a rarity in Jammu’s border zones. On Friday, a balloon bearing the marking of Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) was found near a border post in Ghou Manhasan. This sparked a search of the area as a precautionary measure.
